findings.topic: 1. Go 1.0.18 TreeStore: exact path rule
findings.fact: The path is not a pure function of the ID; it depends on which directories already exist. path() walks successive exact-case 2-character segments ("c4", id[2:4], id[4:6], ...) and descends only while that subdirectory exists, then returns <deepest existing dir>/<full 90-char ID>. A fresh store is therefore FLAT (<store>/<ID>). An object is reachable only in the deepest existing directory on its path. A directory can legitimately hold both subdirectories and loose objects (objects whose next-level directory does not exist yet).
findings.evidence: /Users/joshua/ws/active/software/c4/oss/c4/.worktrees/release-1.0.x/store/treestore.go:347-359 (path). Run: 3 files stored with installed c4 1.0.18 into a new store gave 6 objects all at <store>/<ID> (/tmp/store-layout/compat/fresh-1018). Run: in a store with only c4/41 and c4/4e, new objects c44F... and c44f... landed loose in c4/ (/tmp/store-layout/compat/run2/v2/rel/lay-a).
findings.consequence_for_rule: "Writers put new objects in the deepest directory that exists" is already what every trie writer does. The small-store end is already tidy: zero shard directories up to 4,096 objects. Any new rule that keeps this adaptive start costs nothing at the low end.

findings.topic: 2. Go 1.0.18 split threshold and split behavior
findings.fact: DefaultSplitThreshold = 4096 files per leaf. When a Put pushes a leaf over the threshold, split() moves every non-dot file into a subdirectory named by the next 2 exact-case ID characters. Root splits into the single directory c4/, and the very next Put splits c4/ into the id[2:4] level, so a store jumps from flat to 182 directories at 4,098 objects. Split is not atomic (a loop of renames with errors ignored), is guarded only by an in-process mutex, and moves ANY non-dot file, including non-ID files. Directory names come from sorted ReadDir order, so on a case-insensitive filesystem each letter directory is named by the UPPERCASE form (uppercase sorts first), except i and o, which have no uppercase in base58.
findings.evidence: treestore.go:16 (threshold), :448-465 (noteAdd), :484-506 (split, sub := name[depth:depth+2]). Run: `c4 id -s` of 4,200 files with both binaries gave 0 loose files, 182 directories under c4/, 4,201 objects at depth 2, 39.3% in a directory whose name differs in case from the ID segment (/tmp/store-layout/compat/split-1018, split-master). Directory names seen: 11..19 1A 1B ... 1H 1i 1J ... 1o 1P ...
findings.consequence_for_rule: The "Mac mixed-case trie" is in practice an UPPERCASE-named trie, deterministic rather than random. The 2-character step is very coarse: the next split turns one 4,097-object leaf into up to 1,225 folded (3,364 exact-case) directories of about 3 objects each, which is the "unruly" case Joshua wants to avoid; this starts at roughly 182 x 4,096 = 745k objects. A new rule needs split to skip non-ID names and should not make split a correctness event.

findings.topic: 3. Go 1.0.18 tolerant lookup (locate / foldFind) and its stat cost
findings.fact: locate() stats the exact-case trie path first. On a miss, foldSearch walks from the root trying every ASCII case variant of each 2-character segment (up to 4 per level, exact first, deduplicated with os.SameFile), recursing into each existing variant directory; if any variant directory exists at a level it will not look for the object at that level. Open and Remove use the same fallback. Measured stat calls at depth 2 under case-sensitive emulation: exact hit 4, fold hit 11, miss 12-13 (master: hit 4, miss 3-4).
findings.evidence: treestore.go:365-374 (locate), :385-411 (foldSearch; the `if len(seen) > 0 { return "", false }` line), :426-440 (foldVariants), :123-138 (Open), :314-323 (Remove). Run: /tmp/store-layout/compat/run2/sim1018 (unmodified copy of the 1.0.18 store package driven through its own `stat` test seam) printed Has A=true stats=11, Has B=true stats=4, absent=false stats=12.
findings.consequence_for_rule: 1.0.18 already reads a lowercased trie on any filesystem, at about 3x the stat cost for the roughly 41% of IDs whose segment contains an uppercase letter. Every Put of new content is a miss first, so the fold fallback adds about 8 stats per new object. A lowercased rule makes the fast path exact again and lets foldFind retire to a legacy-only path.

findings.topic: 4. Go 1.0.18 Put on a miss; other Go store types; S3
findings.fact: Put writes a temp file .ingest.* in the store root, then under the lock calls locate(); on a miss it MkdirAll's the parent of the exact-case trie path and renames the temp file there (it never creates a new shard directory outside split). Folder is flat <dir>/<ID>. ShardedFolder is <dir>/<id[3:5]>/<ID>, exact case, with flat read fallback, and is not used by the CLI. MultiStore writes to the first store and reads all stores in order; there is no prefix routing. S3 key is <prefix><full ID>, flat, in both the c4 package and c4d.
findings.evidence: treestore.go:222-294 (Put), folder.go:19-21, sharded.go:20-27 (s[3:5], which skips the third character despite the comment saying characters 3-4), multi.go:23-78, config.go:40-65 (the CLI always uses NewTreeStore or S3), s3store.go:79-81 (s.prefix + id.String()); /Users/joshua/ws/active/software/c4/oss/c4d/internal/store/s3.go:116 (key := id.String()).
findings.consequence_for_rule: S3 needs no layout change (keys are case-sensitive and flat). For the scale requirement, the place where "the same lowercased-prefix rule applied to volumes, buckets or stores" would live is MultiStore plus config.go OpenStore: today it is ordered search, so N stores cost N lookups; prefix routing would be new code. ShardedFolder is a second, incompatible sharding scheme that should be deleted rather than migrated.

findings.topic: 5. Go master (unreleased v1.1) versus 1.0.18
findings.fact: master's treestore.go is identical to 1.0.18 except that it lacks the entire tolerant lookup (no locate, foldFind, foldVariants or stat seam); the 1.0.18 case fix has not been forward-ported. The reported "master writes a flat layout" is true but is not a difference: both versions are flat until 4,097 objects. Real differences: master writes a `journal` file in the store root, `c4 patch` no longer touches directories (`c4 restore --force` materializes), and the master build reports version 1.0.16. sharded.go, folder.go, multi.go, config.go and s3store.go are unchanged.
findings.evidence: diff of /Users/joshua/ws/active/software/c4/oss/c4/store/treestore.go against the release worktree shows only the locate/foldFind additions. Built master (e844612) to /tmp/store-layout/compat/c4-master. Run: new store plus `id -s` gave objects at the store root plus `journal` (/tmp/store-layout/compat/run2/jr-master before the split showed 6 root objects).
findings.consequence_for_rule: Whatever rule is chosen must land on master AND be back-ported or forward-ported consistently. Today master on Linux still has the original 40% bug. The rule must also reserve non-ID names in the store root (journal, log.c4m, .ingest.*).

findings.topic: 6. Bug found on master: the root split moves the journal
findings.fact: When the store root crosses 4,096 objects, split() treats `journal` as an object and moves it to <store>/jo/journal. A new `journal` is then started at the root, and `c4 log` shows only entries written after the split; earlier history is silently dropped from view.
findings.evidence: Run in /tmp/store-layout/compat/run2/jr-master: `c4-master id -s` of a small directory, then of 4,200 files. Root afterwards: c4, jo, journal. jo/journal holds the first claim (c44muHoS...), journal holds only the second (c42VcVkV...), and `c4-master log` lists 1 entry. Cause: treestore.go split() filters only directories and dot-files (master store/treestore.go, same loop as 1.0.18 lines 493-505).
findings.consequence_for_rule: Independent of the layout decision, this is a subtraction-type fix for master: split must move only names that parse as C4 IDs. It also shows that non-ID files do live in store roots (the real default store has log.c4m and three stale .ingest.* files).

findings.topic: 7. c4py
findings.fact: c4py has a directory store, FSStore, that is a line-for-line port of the Go trie: exact-case 2-character walk, deepest existing directory, split at 4,096 using exact-case names. It has no tolerant lookup. Identical on main and the 1.0.x worktree. S3 is not implemented.
findings.evidence: /Users/joshua/ws/active/software/c4/oss/c4py/src/c4py/store.py:149-172 (_resolve_path), :174-201 (_maybe_split, subdir_name = name[depth:depth+2]), :35 (SPLIT_THRESHOLD = 4096), :221 (S3 NotImplementedError). Run against the hand-built stores: reads the lowercased trie at depth 2 and 3 on this Mac, reads nothing in the one-level or two-fixed-level layouts, and does not see objects left above the deepest directory.
findings.consequence_for_rule: Same behavior class as Go master. For a lowercased trie the change is two `.lower()` calls (lines 166 and 198); for an any-depth reader, has()/get() need a loop over levels. On Linux today c4py cannot read 40% of a Mac-built store.

findings.topic: 8. c4ts
findings.fact: The Node TreeStore is already incompatible with every other implementation. It writes <store>/c4/<the 88 characters AFTER "c4"> (the file name drops the c4 prefix), fixed one level, never splits, and reads only that. It cannot read any Go-written store and Go cannot read what it writes. The browser store is IndexedDB keyed by the full ID string (no layout).
findings.evidence: /Users/joshua/ws/active/software/c4/oss/c4ts/packages/node/src/tree-store.ts:70-78 (join(path, s.substring(0,2), s.substring(2))); packages/core/src/browser/store.ts:53-98. Run with the compiled dist (/tmp/store-layout/compat/run2/ts-test.mjs): put wrote c4/4EsxuN... with name length 88; has() returned false on a fresh Go store, a split Go store and the lowercased trie; `c4 cat` on the c4ts store returned content not found.
findings.consequence_for_rule: c4ts must be rewritten whatever is decided, so it imposes no compatibility constraint; it is the strongest argument for a rule simple enough to state in one sentence and test with shared conformance vectors (ID to path).

findings.topic: 9. imgbin (third-party Swift), c4m-swift, libc4
findings.fact: imgbin has a directory store that ports the Go trie walk: exact-case 2-character segments, deepest existing directory, temp file .ingest.<UUID> in the root, rename into place. It never splits and has no tolerant lookup. c4m-swift and libc4 have no store code at all.
findings.evidence: /Users/joshua/ws/active/software/imgbin/Sources/ImgbinCore/Store.swift:68-80 (path(for:)), :98-117 (put). c4m-swift/Sources/C4M contains only c4m types (the only "store" match is a comment in FileMode.swift); libc4/src and libc4/include have no match for "store". imgbin was read, not run (building would write into its tree).
findings.consequence_for_rule: A third-party writer got the trie right by copying 13 lines and skipping split entirely. A rule where split is optional (any-depth validity) makes that the complete, correct implementation: lowercase the segment on line 73 and add the level loop to contentURL. Swift and C need no changes.

findings.topic: 10. c4d, c4git, c4sh, c4-mcp, c4snap
findings.fact: c4d has its own FileStore with a different layout: <root>/<id[3:5]>/<ID>, exact case, one level, flat read fallback, Walk only one level deep, temp files named .c4d-tmp-*. It and the CLI store cannot read each other. c4git, c4sh, c4-mcp and c4snap have no layout code; they call the Go store package (NewTreeStore / OpenStore / OpenConfigured). c4git pins c4 v1.0.16 and c4sh pins a pre-1.0.18 pseudo-version, so neither has the tolerant lookup. c4sh's walkTreeStore walks any depth.
findings.evidence: /Users/joshua/ws/active/software/c4/oss/c4d/internal/store/store.go:68-79 (shardKey s[3:5]), :132-149, :181-225 (Walk); c4git/cmd/c4git/main.go:64-81 and go.mod:6; c4sh/c4mutil.go:50-51, cmd_ingest.go:29 and :99-116, go.mod:6; c4-mcp/tools.go:335; c4snap/cmd/c4snap/main.go:73. Run: both c4 binaries return content not found on a hand-built <root>/Es/<ID> store (/tmp/store-layout/compat/run2/c4d-layout).
findings.consequence_for_rule: The Go-package consumers pick up a new rule by a dependency bump in the suite release. c4d (parked, last commit 2026-03-11) is a third layout that should adopt the shared rule or the shared package when it is revived; nothing written by the CLI is at risk from it today.

findings.topic: 11. Real stores on this Mac (read-only survey)
findings.fact: ~/.c4/store: 194,127 objects, all at depth 2 (c4/XX/<ID>), 182 directories, no deeper level, no loose objects; 75,063 objects (38.7%) sit in a directory whose name differs in case from their ID segment. Root also holds log.c4m and three stale temp files (.ingest.1144815251, .ingest.359728320, .ingest.3284270366, dated Sep 30). The Ash mirror is ~/.ash/c4-init.noindex/store: 64,433 objects, same shape, 24,853 (38.6%) case-mismatched, no leftovers. Directory names are identical in both stores: 52 digit-only, 120 with an UPPERCASE letter, 10 lowercase (1i 1o 2i 2o 3i 3o 4i 4o 5i 5o). The first character of a directory name is 1-6 and names starting with 6 stop at 67, so 182 is the hard maximum for folded id[2:4]. No .c4/store directories were found under ~/ws to depth 7.
findings.evidence: /tmp/store-layout/compat/survey.py run on both stores; ls of ~/.c4/store/c4 and ~/.ash/c4-init.noindex/store/c4 (diff of the two name lists is empty).
findings.consequence_for_rule: Both real stores are exactly "c4/ + toUpper-ish(id[2:4])". Converting them to c4/ + toLower(id[2:4]) is 120 case-only directory renames each and zero object moves. Any rule that drops the c4/ level or changes segment width forces 194,127 object moves instead.

findings.topic: 12. Experiment (a): lowercased 2-character trie on this case-insensitive Mac
findings.fact: Both 1.0.18 and master read and write it correctly. `c4 cat` returned the right bytes for IDs beginning c44E, c44e and c441 stored under c4/4e and c4/41. Materializing worked (1.0.18 `c4 patch target.c4m out-a/` reported 3 created; master `c4 restore --force` likewise). New `c4 id -s` objects beginning c44E and c44e both landed in the existing lowercase c4/4e, with no exact-case sibling and no duplicate when an existing object was stored again. New prefixes with no directory (c44F, c44f) were written loose in c4/.
findings.evidence: /tmp/store-layout/compat/run2/v2-rel.log and v2-master.log; stores in /tmp/store-layout/compat/run2/v2/rel/lay-a and v2/master/lay-a. Depth-3 lowercased layout (c4/4e/sx/<ID>) also read correctly by both (lay-a3).
findings.consequence_for_rule: On case-insensitive filesystems the lowercased trie is fully compatible with every existing trie reader and writer (1.0.18, master, c4py, imgbin). The only drift old writers can introduce there is cosmetic: a later split names new directories in uppercase.

findings.topic: 13. Experiment (a) on a case-sensitive filesystem (emulated, plus code reasoning)
findings.fact: Emulated with a stat function that requires exact-case names (not a real Linux filesystem). 1.0.18: reads everything in the lowercased trie (uppercase-segment IDs through the fallback, 11 stats); re-storing an existing object does not duplicate it; a NEW object whose segment has an uppercase letter (c44E...) is written loose in c4/ because the exact-case directory c4/4E does not exist, and it stays readable there. master: cannot see c44E... objects in c4/4e (Has = false) and on re-store writes a duplicate loose in c4/. Reasoned from code, not run: once 4,097 loose objects accumulate in c4/, split creates exact-case sibling directories (c4/4E beside c4/4e); 1.0.18 still reads both, master, c4py and imgbin read only the exact-case one.
findings.evidence: /tmp/store-layout/compat/run2/sim1018 (unmodified 1.0.18 store package) and /tmp/store-layout/compat/run2/simmaster (master copy with os.Stat routed through a seam, otherwise byte-identical), test sim_test.go, output: sim1018 lower-trie Has A=true/11 stats, tree after Put shows c4/c44EPbVW~ loose and no duplicate of A; simmaster Has A=false, tree shows c4/c44EsxuN~ duplicate. Split naming: treestore.go:501-504.
findings.consequence_for_rule: On Linux, 1.0.18 is a safe reader and a tolerable writer of a lowercased trie (objects stay reachable to it, but about 41% of new objects are misplaced until a new tool tidies them). master, c4py and imgbin as they stand are unsafe there: about 41% of objects invisible, and they duplicate. So the lowercased rule needs the reader fix shipped in all four before any Linux store is normalized.

findings.topic: 14. Experiments (b) and (c): fixed prefix-directory layouts without the c4/ trie
findings.fact: Neither 1.0.18 nor master (nor c4py) can read a store laid out as toLower(id[0:6])/<ID> or as toLower(id[0:4])/toLower(id[4:6])/<ID>: every `c4 cat` returned content not found, on the Mac and under case-sensitive emulation. Existing writers silently duplicate into such a store: `c4 id -s` of an object already present wrote a second copy flat at the store root, and new objects also went to the root; at 4,097 root objects they would be moved into a c4/ trie alongside the new layout.
findings.evidence: /tmp/store-layout/compat/run2/v2-rel.log and v2-master.log sections (b) and (c): after `id -s A`, lay-b contains both c44esx/c44EsxuN~ and ./c44EsxuN~; lay-c contains both c44e/sx/c44EsxuN~ and ./c44EsxuN~. Same result in the sim1018 and simmaster output for the one-level and two-level layouts.
findings.consequence_for_rule: Layouts (b) and (c) are a clean break: no existing reader works, every existing writer forks the store into two layouts, and migration moves every object. They also fail the low-end goal (measured: 120,568 directories for 194,127 objects at 6 characters). They would need a store-format marker that old tools refuse, which old tools do not check for.

findings.topic: 15. The lead's candidate: object valid at any depth along its lowercased path
findings.fact: No existing reader honors it. An object left above the deepest existing directory is invisible to 1.0.18, master and c4py: an object at <store>/<ID> while <store>/c4 exists, or at c4/<ID> while c4/4e exists, returned content not found, and storing it again created a second copy one level deeper. A small flat store copied into a split store loses all of its root-level objects the same way. An object in c4/ whose next directory does not exist IS found. So today a crash in mid-split or an rsync merge of stores at different depths is a correctness event; the candidate would make both valid, and existing writers already satisfy its write rule.
findings.evidence: /tmp/store-layout/compat/run2/v2-rel.log and v2-master.log sections (d) and (m): cat C@root rc=1, cat A@c4 rc=1, cat B@leaf rc=0, cat N5@c4,no-subdir rc=0; after `id -s` the tree holds both ./c4412gW3~ and c4/c4412gW3~. Reader logic: treestore.go:347-359 and the `len(seen) > 0` return at :402-404.
findings.consequence_for_rule: The claim is true as a design and is a pure reader-side addition: on a miss at the deepest directory, also check <dir>/<ID> at each shallower level. Derived cost (not run): a hit is unchanged (4 stats at depth 2); a miss costs one extra stat per level (6 at depth 2), versus 12-13 for the 1.0.18 fold fallback today. Two things must change with it: Remove has to delete the object at every level or a shallower duplicate resurrects it (treestore.go:314-323 removes one path), and anything counting via Walk must tolerate the same ID twice. It also lets c4py, c4ts and Swift omit split entirely.

findings.topic: 16. Migration cost for each existing layout
findings.fact: Mac uppercase-named trie to lowercased trie: rename-only, one case-only rename per directory, no object moves. Measured on a 4,201-object, 182-directory copy: 120 directory renames in 0.05 s, after which 300 of 300 sampled objects read back with both binaries and a further 1.0.18 `id -s` created no uppercase directory and no loose file. Linux exact-case trie to lowercased trie: rename-only but per object, merging each uppercase sibling directory into its lowercase one (about 41% of objects, same filesystem, no data copied); the script handles this branch but it was not run on a real case-sensitive filesystem. master's layout is the same as 1.0.18's (flat below 4,097 objects, trie above), so no separate migration. Flat stores need nothing under an adaptive rule. To layouts (b) or (c): every object moves (194,127 renames plus up to 120,568 mkdirs for the default store) and old tools must be locked out.
findings.evidence: /tmp/store-layout/compat/run2/normalize.py run on /tmp/store-layout/compat/run2/norm (a copy of /tmp/store-layout/compat/split-1018): "dir renames: 120 file moves: 0 seconds: 0.052", then c4: cat ok=300 fail=0, c4-master: cat ok=300 fail=0.
findings.consequence_for_rule: Cheapest path: keep c4/ and 2-character segments, lowercase the names, normalize opportunistically (a store can be normalized in place while old Mac tools keep using it), and keep a tolerant read for legacy case variants only as long as un-normalized stores exist. Tolerant-read-forever is not required on the Mac; on Linux it is required until the store is normalized and all writers are updated.

findings.topic: 17. Code changes per implementation, by candidate
findings.fact: Lowercased adaptive trie: Go treestore.go path() (lowercase str[i:i+2]) and split() (lowercase the subdirectory name, move only names that parse as IDs), plus forward-porting locate/foldFind to master as the legacy reader; c4py store.py _resolve_path line 166 and _maybe_split line 198; imgbin Store.swift path(for:) line 73; c4ts tree-store.ts idToPath/idToDir lines 70-78 (full rewrite, it is wrong today); c4d internal/store/store.go shardKey/shardPath lines 68-75 or switch to the shared package; delete c4 store/sharded.go. Adding any-depth validity: Go locate(), Open(), Remove(), Walk dedupe; c4py has()/get(); imgbin contentURL(); c4ts has()/get()/remove(); split becomes optional outside Go. Fixed layouts (b)/(c): path becomes a one-line pure function in each of the same places and all trie-walk and split code is deleted, but every store needs a mover, a legacy reader for the old trie, and a guard against old writers. c4git, c4sh, c4-mcp, c4snap: go.mod bump only. c4m-swift and libc4: nothing.
findings.evidence: File and line references in findings 1-10; behavior of each change point verified by the runs in findings 12-15.
findings.consequence_for_rule: The lowercased trie is about two lines per trie implementation plus one shared set of ID-to-path conformance vectors. Any-depth adds a short loop per reader and removes the need for split in four of five implementations. Docs to update when the rule lands: store/README.md, ARCHITECTURAL_CATALOG.md line 208, CHANGELOG, and the layout comments at the top of c4py store.py and c4ts tree-store.ts.

ground:compat.summary:
Lowercasing the existing 2-character trie directory names is the only candidate that existing tools can already read and that migrates by rename alone; the two fixed prefix layouts break every reader and make every existing writer duplicate. All claims below were run on this Mac except where marked; case-sensitive behavior was emulated with an exact-case stat function, not a real Linux filesystem.

**What exists today**
- **Go 1.0.18 and master:** identical adaptive trie. Flat at the store root up to 4,096 objects, then `c4/<id[2:4]>/<ID>` (182 directories), with each leaf splitting again above 4,096. An object is found only in the deepest existing directory on its path.
- **master lacks the 1.0.18 case fix.** Its `treestore.go` is 1.0.18 minus `locate`/`foldFind`. The "master writes flat" report is true but is not a difference; 1.0.18 does the same.
- **c4py and imgbin:** exact-case ports of the trie with no tolerant lookup. imgbin never splits.
- **c4ts:** already incompatible with everything. It writes `c4/<88 characters without the c4 prefix>`; Go cannot read it and it cannot read Go stores.
- **c4d:** its own layout, `<root>/<id[3:5]>/<ID>`, unreadable by the CLI and vice versa.
- **c4m-swift and libc4:** no store code. c4git, c4sh, c4-mcp and c4snap use the Go package; c4git and c4sh pin versions older than 1.0.18.
- **S3:** flat `<prefix><ID>` keys, no change needed.
- **Real stores:** `~/.c4/store` (194,127 objects) and `~/.ash/c4-init.noindex/store` (64,433) are both exactly `c4/XX/<ID>` with 182 directories. 120 names are uppercase because split names directories in sorted order; about 38.7% of objects sit under a name that differs in case from their ID.

**Which reader can read which layout**

| Layout | 1.0.18 | master, c4py, imgbin (imgbin by code reading) | c4ts |
|---|---|---|---|
| Lowercased trie, Mac | yes (run) | yes (master and c4py run) | no |
| Lowercased trie, case-sensitive | yes, 11 stats instead of 4 for uppercase segments | about 41% invisible | no |
| `toLower(id[0:6])/<ID>` | no | no | no |
| `toLower(id[0:4])/toLower(id[4:6])/<ID>` | no | no | no |

**What existing writers do to each layout**
- **Lowercased trie on the Mac:** correct. `c4 cat`, `c4 patch` (1.0.18) and `c4 restore --force` (master) work; new `c4 id -s` objects for c44E and c44e both land in `c4/4e` with no sibling and no duplicate.
- **Lowercased trie on a case-sensitive filesystem:** 1.0.18 writes new uppercase-segment objects loose in `c4/` (still readable to it). master, c4py and imgbin duplicate existing objects there. A later split would create exact-case sibling directories (reasoned from `treestore.go:501-504`, not run).
- **Either fixed layout:** every existing writer puts a second copy flat at the store root.

**The any-depth candidate**
- No existing reader honors it: an object left above the deepest directory returned "content not found" in 1.0.18, master and c4py, and re-storing it made a deeper duplicate.
- So today a crash in mid-split, or rsync of a small flat store into a split one, loses objects from view. The candidate fixes that with a reader-only change.
- Existing writers already follow its write rule.
- Derived cost, not run: a hit is unchanged at 4 stats; a miss is about 6 at depth 2, against 12-13 for the 1.0.18 fallback.
- It requires `Remove` to delete at every level and `Walk` consumers to tolerate duplicates. It lets every non-Go implementation skip split.

**Migration**
- **Mac stores:** 120 case-only directory renames, no object moves. On a 4,201-object test copy this took 0.05 s, and 300 of 300 sampled objects read back with both binaries.
- **Linux exact-case stores:** merge uppercase sibling directories into lowercase ones, per-object renames with no data copied. Not run on a real case-sensitive filesystem.
- **Fixed layouts:** move all 194,127 objects and lock out old tools.

**Bug found on master, separate from the layout decision**
When the root crosses 4,096 objects, split moves the `journal` file to `<store>/jo/journal` and `c4 log` loses the earlier entries. Reproduced in `/tmp/store-layout/compat/run2/jr-master`. Split should move only names that parse as C4 IDs.

**Scale notes from this angle**
- The 2-character step is coarse: a 4,097-object leaf splits into up to 1,225 lowercased directories of about 3 objects each, starting near 745k objects.
- `MultiStore` is ordered search with no prefix routing, so applying the same prefix rule to volumes or buckets would be new code in `store/multi.go` and `store/config.go`.

**Housekeeping**
- An earlier run with this label left files in `/tmp/store-layout/compat/`. One of my first store names (`a-master`) collided with its `A-master` on this case-insensitive disk; I discarded that result and reran everything under `/tmp/store-layout/compat/run2/`.
- No repo and neither real store was modified.
- Main logs: `run2/v2-rel.log`, `run2/v2-master.log`, and the emulation output from `run2/sim1018` and `run2/simmaster`.

ground:portability.summary:
Lowercased shard directory names are safe on every filesystem, transport and sync tool I checked. The only layout that is both name-safe and without a per-directory ceiling is the adaptive trie of 2-character lowercased levels with the 4096 split threshold.

**What was run on this Mac (case-insensitive APFS), under `/tmp/store-layout/portability/`:**
- c4 1.0.18 built a store of 6,401 objects: 182 shard dirs, 120 with non-lowercase names, 39.8% of objects in a dir whose name is not their exact-case `id[2:4]`.
- A tar and a zip of the same objects in a case-sensitive layout (297 exact-case dirs) extracted with exit 0 and no warning into 182 merged dirs, all 6,401 files present. `rsync -a` and `cp -R` merge the same way.
- `rsync -a --delete-after` and `--delete-delay` between two trees whose shard dir differs only in case (`1j` vs `1J`) deleted the whole shard at the destination, exit 0. This happened with both rsync 3.5.0 and Apple's openrsync.
- A copy of the store with all 120 dirs renamed to lowercase was read (400 of 400 sampled) and written (800 more objects, no uppercase dir created) by c4 1.0.18.
- Under the release's own case-sensitive stat emulation, 1.0.18 reads an all-lowercase store, but writes a new uppercase-prefix object into the interior `c4/` directory.

**Per-candidate verdict:**

| Candidate | Names safe everywhere | Ceiling / problem |
|---|---|---|
| `toLower(id[0:4])`, one level (≤182 dirs) | Yes | FAT32 fails at 8,191 objects per dir (about 1.5M objects); exFAT at 1,048,576 per dir with linear scans long before; ext4 htree at roughly 7–10M per dir |
| `toLower(id[0:5])`, one level (≤6,370 dirs) | Yes | Same per-dir ceilings, 35x later; 6,370 dirs for a small store |
| `toLower(id[0:6])`, one level (≤222,950 dirs in one parent) | Yes | Exceeds FAT32's 65,536 entries per directory and ext3's 32,000 subdirs; 120k dirs holding about one object each at 194k objects |
| Two fixed 2-char levels | Yes | Each parent ≤1,225 entries, so safe; but about 120k leaf dirs at 194k objects, and still a ceiling |
| Adaptive 2-char lowercased trie, threshold 4096 | Yes | None from the layout; 3 levels below `c4/` at 10^12 objects, 12 extra path characters |

**Constraints the rule should state:**
- Keep every level below the first at exactly 2 characters. A 3-character deeper level can spell `con`, `prn`, `aux`, `nul`; a 4-character one can spell `com1`–`com9`, `lpt1`–`lpt9`. The first level is safe at any width because it starts with `c4` or a digit 1–6.
- Fold to lowercase, not uppercase, and ASCII-only. Base58 has no `I`, so lowercasing is locale-proof; uppercasing `i` gives `İ` under Turkish and Azeri locales.
- Keep the split threshold at or below about 7,800 if FAT32 is a target; 4096 has 2x margin. On FAT32 the split is mandatory, not an optimisation.
- Windows MAX_PATH is not binding: the store root can be up to about 156 characters at 4 levels.

**Where one filesystem stops:** ext4 and NTFS cap at about 4.29 billion files per filesystem, so 10^12 objects cannot live on one ext4 or NTFS volume under any layout. Beyond that it is XFS/ZFS, multiple volumes keyed by the same lowercased prefix, or an object store. On S3 the key is the exact-case ID (as `s3store.go` does today); the lowercased prefix only matters if a bucket is mirrored file-for-file to a filesystem.

**Migration hazard:** stores must be normalised by c4 on each machine. Plain rsync keeps the old-case names at the destination, and rsync with `--delete-after` wipes the shard. A case-only rename works in place on APFS. A case-sensitive store that already holds both `4e/` and `4E/` needs a merge instead.

**Not verified:**
- No real case-sensitive filesystem, Windows machine, FAT/exFAT volume, SMB/NFS share or cloud sync client was available (Docker was down; disk images and remotes were off-limits). Those behaviours are from documentation or the emulation.
- Finder and Explorer were not driven.
- The APFS timings are warm-cache with empty files.
- The directory `/tmp/store-layout/portability/` also contains `exp1`, `exp2`, `s1`, `s2`, `src4200` that I did not create.

findings.topic: Windows reserved device names vs candidate shard names
findings.fact: The folded base58 alphabet is 1-9 plus a-z (35 symbols), so con, prn, aux, nul, com1-9 and lpt1-9 are all spellable. No 2-character name can be reserved. No name starting with 'c4' can be reserved. A first-level name without 'c4' starts with a digit 1-6, so it cannot be reserved at 3 or 4 characters either. Deeper levels are the risk: a 3-character level can equal con/prn/aux/nul (4 of 42,875 names), and a 4-character level can equal com1-9/lpt1-9 (18 of 1,500,625). The object file name (90 characters, starts 'c4') is never reserved.
findings.evidence: Computed in /tmp/store-layout/portability (python enumeration of the alphabet against the reserved list). Reserved list and 'also avoid these names followed immediately by an extension' from https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/fileio/naming-a-file . com0/lpt0 need '0', which base58 lacks.
findings.consequence_for_rule: State in the rule that every level below the first is exactly 2 characters. Any first-level width (c4, c4xx, c4xxx, c4xxxx, or xx) is safe. A second or deeper level of 3 or 4 characters is not safe on Windows, NTFS-backed SMB shares, or OneDrive.

findings.topic: Trailing dot/space, Unicode normalization, locale folding
findings.fact: Base58 has no dot or space, so the Windows trailing-dot/space rule cannot apply. The alphabet is pure ASCII: NFC, NFD, NFKC and NFKD are all identity on it, and casefold equals lower. Lowercasing is locale-proof because base58 has no uppercase 'I'. Uppercasing is not: 'i' becomes 'İ' under tr and az locales.
findings.evidence: Run: python unicodedata.normalize over the alphabet returned identity for all four forms. Run: node toLocaleLowerCase('tr'|'az'|'lt') matched toLowerCase for all 58 characters; toLocaleUpperCase differed for 'i' under tr and az. Trailing dot/space rule from https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/fileio/naming-a-file .
findings.consequence_for_rule: Fold to lowercase, never uppercase, and specify it as ASCII A-Z to a-z only. Every one of the five implementations then gets the same bytes without locale handling. Unicode normalization on APFS/HFS+ is irrelevant.

findings.topic: Case behaviour of filesystems and network exports
findings.fact: Case-insensitive but case-preserving: APFS default, HFS+ default, NTFS (Win32 namespace), exFAT, FAT32 with long names, SMB shares as seen by Windows and macOS clients. Case-sensitive: ext4, XFS, btrfs, ZFS default, case-sensitive APFS. But 'case-sensitive' filesystems can be made insensitive: ext4 casefold per directory (chattr +F, Linux 5.2+), ZFS casesensitivity=insensitive|mixed, XFS ascii-ci (deprecated). NTFS can be made case-sensitive per directory, and WSL-created directories are. NFS inherits the server filesystem's behaviour; a Linux client must disable negative-dentry caching for a case-insensitive export.
findings.evidence: exFAT 'case insensitive and case preserving': https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/fileio/exfat-specification . NTFS: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NTFS . ext4 casefold: https://www.collabora.com/news-and-blog/blog/2020/08/27/using-the-linux-kernel-case-insensitive-feature-in-ext4/ . ZFS: https://docs.oracle.com/en/operating-systems/solaris/oracle-solaris/11.4/manage-zfs/casesensitivity-property.html . XFS: https://linux.die.net/man/8/mkfs.xfs . btrfs sensitive only: https://github.com/btrfs/btrfs-todo/issues/44 . Windows per-directory: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/case-sensitivity . NFS: https://ratatoskr.run/linux-nfs/2026/04/348385/t
findings.consequence_for_rule: Case sensitivity cannot be inferred from the OS or the filesystem type, so a rule that depends on detecting it is unsound. A lowercase-only name is the same directory under every one of these behaviours, and a client never issues a lookup in another case. 'For all filesystems regardless' is the right scope.

findings.topic: What 1.0.18 does today on a case-insensitive Mac
findings.fact: A store starts flat (<store>/<ID>) and splits past 4096 into c4/ and then c4/xx/. After the split, 120 of 182 shard directories had non-lowercase names, and 39.8% of objects sat in a directory whose name is not their exact-case id[2:4]. Extracted or copied verbatim to a case-sensitive filesystem, those are the objects a strict exact-case reader cannot reach.
findings.evidence: Run with C4_STORE=/tmp/store-layout/portability/c4mac/store: 'c4 src' on 6,000 small files plus 400 piped objects gave 6,401 objects; ls store/c4 showed 182 dirs, 120 containing an uppercase letter; python count found 2,546 of 6,401 misfiled.
findings.consequence_for_rule: Reproduces the reported roughly 40% and the 120-of-182 figure on a fresh store. The defect is the first-arrival spelling of the directory name, which a fixed lowercase spelling removes.

findings.topic: tar, zip, ditto, cp -R, rsync: case-sensitive tree onto a case-insensitive filesystem
findings.fact: A tree with both '1j/' and '1J/' collapses silently into one directory named by whichever arrived first. No tool warned or failed, and no object was lost because the object file names are distinct. The same archive would extract on Linux as separate exact-case directories.
findings.evidence: Run in /tmp/store-layout/portability/tarx: python tarfile/zipfile built an archive of 6,401 real objects under 297 exact-case dirs. '/usr/bin/tar -xf', 'unzip -q' and 'ditto -x -k' each exited 0 and produced 182 dirs, 6,401 files, 120 uppercase-named. In rs/: 'rsync -a A2/1J B2/1j dst/' (rsync 3.5.0 and openrsync) and 'cp -R A2/1J B2/1j dst/' each produced one dir '1J' holding all three files.
findings.consequence_for_rule: Linux to Mac is lossless but changes the tree; Mac to Linux preserves whatever case the Mac happened to choose. Only a canonical spelling makes the two directions identical. Under the lowercase rule every one of these tools is an exact, order-independent union.

findings.topic: rsync --delete-after / --delete-delay destroys a shard when directory case differs
findings.fact: With source 'c4/1j/' and destination 'c4/1J/' on a case-insensitive destination, rsync transfers into the existing directory and then deletes 'c4/1J/' as extraneous, including the files it just wrote. Exit status is 0. A second run restores it. Plain --delete, --delete-before and --delete-during delete first and recreate the directory as '1j', which is correct. Plain 'rsync -a' merges but leaves the old-case name '1J'.
findings.evidence: Run in /tmp/store-layout/portability/rs/r3: '/opt/homebrew/bin/rsync -a --delete-after -i src/ dst/' printed '>f+++++++++ c4/1j/objB', then '*deleting c4/1J/objC', '*deleting c4/1J/objB', '*deleting c4/1J/objA', '*deleting c4/1J/', exit 0, leaving dst/c4 empty. Same result for --delete-delay, and for /usr/bin/rsync (openrsync, protocol 29). rsync's own man page warns about case-ignoring destinations: https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/rsync.1.html
findings.consequence_for_rule: This is silent data loss in a mirror, and by the same mechanism it applies today between any two case-insensitive stores whose shard names differ in case (two Macs populated in different order). It is the strongest argument for normalising existing stores. Normalisation must be done by c4 on each store, because plain rsync does not carry the new spelling across.

findings.topic: Normalising an existing store, and compatibility with released 1.0.18
findings.fact: On APFS a case-only rename works in place. A store with all shard dirs lowercased is fully readable and writable by c4 1.0.18 on the Mac. Under case-sensitive emulation, 1.0.18 also reads the lowercase store through its fold lookup, but writes a new object whose exact-case segment directory is absent into the interior directory c4/. By reading the code (not run): past 4096 such files it would split c4/ into exact-case directories, recreating '4W' beside '4w'. Master (unreleased v1.1) has no fold lookup in store/ at all.
findings.evidence: Run: 'mv ren/c4/1J ren/c4/1j' and python os.rename both succeeded. Run in norm/: 120 dirs renamed, 400 of 400 sampled 'c4 cat' succeeded, 800 more objects stored, still 182 dirs with 0 uppercase-named. Run: go test in a scratch copy of the release worktree (/tmp/store-layout/portability/c4src/store/zz_portability_test.go) using the release's caseSensitiveStat seam logged Has=true, Open ok, ContentPath=c4/4w/..., and 'WRITE new id c44WJhpX... landed at c4'. grep for foldVariants in master's store/ returned nothing.
findings.consequence_for_rule: Normalising Mac stores is safe against the released reader. On Linux, 1.0.18 writing into a normalised store leaves objects at a shallower level of their own prefix path. That is valid under the lead's any-depth invariant and invalid under a strict fixed-level rule, which is a point for the any-depth invariant. Case-sensitive stores that already hold both spellings need a merge, not a rename, and new readers must still probe legacy exact-case directories until then.

findings.topic: Per-directory limits with a 90-character name
findings.fact: FAT32: a 90-character name takes 8 directory entries (7 long-name plus 1 short), so the 65,536-entry cap is 8,191 objects per directory. exFAT: 8 entries (256 bytes) per object against a 256 MB directory cap is 1,048,576 objects per directory, and lookups scan the directory linearly, helped only by a 16-bit name hash. ext4: about 10-12M entries with the default 2-level htree, fewer with 100-byte entries; large_dir raises it; without dir_index lookups are linear. ext3 allows 32,000 subdirectories and ext4 about 65,000 without dir_nlink. NTFS, XFS, ZFS and APFS have no practical per-directory limit.
findings.evidence: Arithmetic run in python: ceil(90/13)+1 = 8 and (65536-2)//8 = 8191; (2+ceil(90/15))*32 = 256 bytes and 256 MiB/256 = 1,048,576. FAT: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Design_of_the_FAT_file_system . exFAT 256 MB and 2,796,202 for minimal names: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ExFAT . ext4: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ext4 and https://utcc.utoronto.ca/~cks/space/blog/linux/Ext4DirectoriesMaximumSize . Subdirectory limits: https://access.redhat.com/solutions/20913
findings.consequence_for_rule: Any fixed single level has a hard ceiling: id[0:4] fails on FAT32 near 1.5M objects and on exFAT near 190M. id[0:6] can need 222,950 directories in one parent, which exceeds FAT32's entry cap and ext3's subdirectory cap. The adaptive trie at threshold 4096 keeps every directory at or below 4096 files plus 1,225 subdirectories, under every limit. On FAT32 the split is mandatory before about 7,800 files, so there it is a correctness event, not only an optimisation.

findings.topic: Practical performance: APFS measured, SMB and NFS from documentation
findings.fact: On local APFS, 200,000 objects in one flat directory performed as well as any sharded layout, so APFS itself does not force sharding at that size. The 6-character layout was the slowest: 120,812 directories and a full walk 35 times slower than the 4-character layout. Samba emulating case-insensitivity over a case-sensitive filesystem must scan the whole directory to decide a name is absent; its documentation recommends all-lowercase names for directories above 100,000 files.
findings.evidence: Run (python, empty files, warm cache): flat: create 48 us, stat-hit 1.9 us, full walk 0.14 s. toLower(id[0:4]), 175 dirs: 52 us, 3.1 us, 0.11 s. id[0:5], 6,125 dirs: 58 us, 5.8 us, 0.27 s. id[0:6], 120,812 dirs: 77 us, 11.5 us, 3.91 s. Samba: https://wiki.samba.org/index.php/Performance_Tuning and https://www.samba.org/samba/docs/current/man-html/smb.conf.5.html
findings.consequence_for_rule: For the small end, fewer directories is both tidier and faster; id[0:6] is the worst choice on both counts. Small bounded directories matter for exFAT, Samba and network listing rather than for APFS. All-lowercase names are also what lets a Samba admin turn the scan off.

findings.topic: MAX_PATH on Windows
findings.fact: The Win32 limit is 260 characters including the terminator, unless the app opts in to long paths or uses the \\?\ prefix. Go's os package adds the prefix automatically; Python, Node, Swift and C do not unless long paths are enabled. The trie adds 3 characters per level: at 10^12 objects the path is root + '\c4' + 3 levels + '\' + 90, which is root + 103 characters.
findings.evidence: Depth computed in python at 4096 per leaf with fan-out 182 then 1,225: 1 level at 2e5 objects, 2 at 1e6, 3 at 1e9 and 1e12, 4 at 1e15, 5 at 1e18. Limits: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/fileio/maximum-file-path-limitation . Go: https://go.dev/src/os/path_windows.go
findings.consequence_for_rule: Not binding for any candidate. With 4 levels including c4, the store root may be up to about 156 characters. Temp files should be no longer than the 90-character final name so the temp path is never the longest one.

findings.topic: Finder and Windows Explorer
findings.fact: Finder offers Replace when a same-named folder exists (matching case-insensitively), and Replace deletes the destination folder's contents. Merge appears only with Option-drag and only in some conditions. Explorer on Windows 10/11 merges same-named folders silently by default. In a per-directory case-sensitive NTFS folder, Explorer shows both spellings but opens only one.
findings.evidence: Not run (no GUI automation). Finder: https://eshop.macsales.com/blog/80383-merging-folders-in-macos/ . Explorer: https://www.windowsdigitals.com/no-duplicate-warning-when-copy-move-paste-files-folders-windows-10/ . Per-directory case: https://devblogs.microsoft.com/commandline/per-directory-case-sensitivity-and-wsl/
findings.consequence_for_rule: Explorer merging is a correct union under any consistent layout. Finder's Replace is a hazard for hand-merging stores under every layout and is not solved by the rule; it belongs in the docs as 'merge stores with rsync or c4, not by dragging'.

findings.topic: Cloud sync tools and case conflicts
findings.fact: Each tool breaks a store that contains two directories differing only in case. Dropbox renames one to 'name (Case Conflict)'. OneDrive cannot hold both, and the Linux client refuses to sync the conflicting item. iCloud Drive bounces the newcomer to 'name 2'. Syncthing (1.9+) raises a case-conflict error and does not sync the second. rclone to a Mac or Windows target logs 'Duplicate object found in source - ignoring'.
findings.evidence: Not run. Dropbox: https://help.dropbox.com/organize/case-conflict . OneDrive: https://github.com/abraunegg/onedrive/blob/master/docs/usage.md . iCloud: https://developer.apple.com/library/archive/technotes/tn2336/_index.html . Syncthing: https://docs.syncthing.net/advanced/folder-caseSensitiveFS.html . rclone: https://rclone.org/overview/
findings.consequence_for_rule: Every failure needs a both-case pair, which only an exact-case layout on a case-sensitive filesystem produces. Under the lowercase rule no such pair can exist. Two object files could collide only if two IDs were equal under folding, which is a 35^88 (about 2^451) space.

findings.topic: Object stores (S3)
findings.fact: S3 keys are exact-case byte strings with no directories and no per-prefix entry limit. S3 scales request rate per prefix automatically (at least 3,500 writes and 5,500 reads per second per prefix), and since 2018 no prefix randomisation is needed. The released S3Store already uses the flat key prefix + full ID.
findings.evidence: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-keys.html and https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/optimizing-performance.html . Code read, not run: store/s3store.go line 79-80, objectKey returns s.prefix + id.String().
findings.consequence_for_rule: On an object store the rule is its depth-zero case: the key is the exact-case ID, discoverable with no tool. Lowercased-prefix keys ('c4/4e/<ID>') are only worth using if a bucket must mirror file-for-file to a filesystem with 'aws s3 sync' or rclone. Under the any-depth invariant a flat bucket synced to disk is already a valid, unsplit store. The same lowercased prefix can name buckets or volumes when one store is partitioned.

findings.topic: Where one filesystem stops (the 10^12 requirement)
findings.fact: ext4 holds at most about 4 billion files per filesystem, fixed at creation, and NTFS at most 2^32-1 per volume. So 10^12 objects cannot live on one ext4 or NTFS filesystem under any layout; it would take at least 233 of them. FAT32 also caps a file at 4 GiB - 1, which rules it out for large media objects.
findings.evidence: ext4 'Max number of files: 4 billion (specified at filesystem creation time)': https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ext4 . NTFS '4,294,967,295 (2^32-1)': https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NTFS . Trie depth computed: 3 levels below c4/ at 10^12, 5 at 10^18. The FAT32 file-size limit is from memory and was not looked up today.
findings.consequence_for_rule: The adaptive 2-character trie has no ceiling of its own; the filesystem's file count is the ceiling, at about 4.29e9 on ext4 and NTFS. Past that the organisation is XFS or ZFS, several volumes each owning a set of lowercased prefixes (the same rule applied one level up), or an object store keyed by the ID.

findings.topic: A third exact-case layout exists in the released tree
findings.fact: store/sharded.go (ShardedFolder) shards by exact-case s[3:5] with a flat fallback, giving up to 3,364 directories. Its comment says 'characters 3-4' but the slice is the 4th and 5th characters. store/folder.go is a flat layout. Together with TreeStore that is three layouts in one package, two of them exact-case.
findings.evidence: Code read, not run: /Users/joshua/ws/active/software/c4/oss/c4/.worktrees/release-1.0.x/store/sharded.go lines 13-27 and store/folder.go. I did not check which callers use ShardedFolder.
findings.consequence_for_rule: Whatever rule is adopted must also cover or delete ShardedFolder, or the same Mac-to-Linux defect survives in that code path. Under the any-depth invariant, Folder (flat) is simply depth zero and needs no separate concept.
